The brief facts are these:
The petitioner Firm had filed an application on 11.03.2006 to the Karnataka Udyog Mithra seeking approval for the establishment of a "Business Process Outsourcing,
Offshore Development Centre and Software Development and Service Center" from Mangalore's proposed IT City and sought for allotment of an extent of 40,470 square meters of land at Kairangala, Pajeer Villages at Mangalore along with other infrastructure facilities like power, water, etc.

The Karnataka Udyog Mithra addressed a letter dated 03.04.2006 to the petitioner, intimating that the project proposal was considered by the State Level Single Window Clearance Committee on 20.03.2006 and the same had been approved by providing the infrastructural assistance as set out in the letter therein.

The Committee resolved to recommend to KIADB to issue a letter of intent for 10 Acres of land being acquired by KIADB at Pajeer,
Kairangala, Koornadu Villages in Mangalore.
A quantity of 3,00,000 LPD of water was assured to be supplied by KIADB and 250 KVA power was assured to be serviced by MESCOM.

sentences.text: Heard, the contentions urged on behalf of the respective parties and perused the Writ papers and also the Annexures with utmost care.

5. The following short point would arise for my consideration:
Is the action of the Industrial Board justified?

The first argument, in the present case,
is centered around that the Board being the Promisor has by its promise created a reasonable expectation that it will adhere to the commitment to provide basic infrastructure facilities to set up the project, but it failed to keep up the obligation and the second is about the unilateral cancellation of the allotment of plots for the alleged violation of the terms and conditions contained in the allotment letter.
Before answering the point let us quickly glance through the simple meaning of infrastructure.
The term infrastructure first appeared in the late 1880s, derived from French, with infra- meaning below and structure meaning building.
Infrastructure can mean the foundation upon which the structure of an economy is built.

Whether in the private or public sector, precise planning and finely-tuned strategies are necessary to overcome the challenges faced by modern infrastructure projects.
More importantly, careful consideration of the human element as well as the economic impacts is required for these essential projects.
For this reason, it's worth clarifying the logistics and challenges professionals need to balance to succeed in infrastructure project management.
Infrastructure is crucially an important sector for the overall development of any country.
Suffice it to note that the State of Karnataka with a laudable object for the establishment of an Industrial Area has constituted the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB).
The KIADB is a statutory body established under the provisions of the KIAD Act of 1966 to promote the establishment and orderly development of industries in industrial areas.
The State Government issued Notifications under the provisions of the KIAD Act, as an Industrial Area in several lands situated at Pajeeru and Kariangala villages of Bantwals Taluk, Dakshina Kannada.

As already noted above, the whole controversy revolves around the alleged violations of the terms and conditions.
Learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Board strenuously urged regarding the violations of the terms and conditions of the contract.
To answer this query, the Board must consider the following points.
Is there a contract?
Whether the terms and conditions of the allotment letter amount to the formation of a contract?
Can the allotment letter be construed as a concluded contract?
It is well established that a contract is a promise or set of promises which the law will enforce.

The main justification for the legal enforcement of promise is an economic one: trade and commerce would be impossible if the law permitted a promisor to break his promise without, at least, placing him under an obligation to pay compensation for the loss occasioned by his default.

But a moral justification has also been put forward as - 23 - M/S Chantilly Group vs State Of Karnataka on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82607139/
10 the basis of the law of contract, in that the promisor has by his promise created a reasonable expectation that it will be kept.

sentences.text: The law, therefore, recognizes a moral duty in the promisor to keep his promise and attempts the realization of the reasonable expectations that have been induced by the making of the promise.
Common sense suggests that the law has long recognized that the obligations created by a contract are not all of equal importance.
It is primarily for the parties to set their value on the terms that they impose upon each other.

But it is rare for them to express with any precision what, if anything, they have in their minds; and the resultant ask for inferring and interpreting their intention is, as always,
a matter of great difficulty.

sentences.text: It is not in dispute that the meeting was held on the 7th day of December 2010 regarding providing infrastructural facilities.
It is interesting to note that due to the delay in providing infrastructural facilities, it was decided to extend the time for the payment of the balance cost of the land without any interest.
The Board indeed extended the timeline for the payment of the balance amount.
It has given the go-by to the terms and conditions.
Under these circumstances, the action of the Board is not justified.

The main justification for the legal enforcement of the right by the petitioner is that the Board was under an obligation to provide the infrastructure facilities but it failed to keep up the obligation even after the extension of time.
In my considered view, the petitioner is right in its justification.
There is nothing on record to show that the Board informed the petitioner about the completion of the infrastructure facilities.
On the other hand, it went on demanding the payment of the balance amount with interest.
And on one fine day, it informed the petitioner that it has canceled the allotment of land in plots No.2 Part & 3 with immediate effect.
The Board also informed the petitioner to go over to their office for a refund of the eligible amount as per the rules.

I may venture to say that the Board has utterly failed to keep up its promise.
Hence, the cancellation is bad.
Furthermore, the Board in the allotment - 27 - letter, has agreed to refund the eligible amount to the petitioner.

opennyai_summary.issue:
5. The following short point would arise for my consideration:
Is the action of the Industrial Board justified?
The first argument, in the present case,
is centered around that the Board being the Promisor has by its promise created a reasonable expectation that it will adhere to the commitment to provide basic infrastructure facilities to set up the project, but it failed to keep up the obligation and the second is about the unilateral cancellation of the allotment of plots for the alleged violation of the terms and conditions contained in the allotment letter.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Infrastructure is crucially an important sector for the overall development of any country.
The KIADB is a statutory body established under the provisions of the KIAD Act of 1966 to promote the establishment and orderly development of industries in industrial areas.
The State Government issued Notifications under the provisions of the KIAD Act, as an Industrial Area in several lands situated at Pajeeru and Kariangala villages of Bantwals Taluk, Dakshina Kannada.
The State Government - 15 - issued Notifications under Sections 28(1) and 28(4) of the Land Acquisition Act and transferred the lands to KIADB.
It is well established that a contract is a promise or set of promises which the law will enforce.
The main justification for the legal enforcement of promise is an economic one: trade and commerce would be impossible if the law permitted a promisor to break his promise without, at least, placing him under an obligation to pay compensation for the loss occasioned by his default.
But a moral justification has also been put forward as - 23 - M/S Chantilly Group vs State Of Karnataka on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82607139/
10 the basis of the law of contract, in that the promisor has by his promise created a reasonable expectation that it will be kept.
The law, therefore, recognizes a moral duty in the promisor to keep his promise and attempts the realization of the reasonable expectations that have been induced by the making of the promise.
It is primarily for the parties to set their value on the terms that they impose upon each other.
The tentative price of the land per acre was fixed at Rs.30,00,000/- (Rupees Thirty Lakh only).
Condition No.6(a) refers to the automatic expiry M/S Chantilly Group vs State Of Karnataka on 20 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/82607139/
11 of the offer of allotment and forfeiture of the earnest money deposit and 25% of the amount paid towards the cost of the land.
It is not in dispute that the meeting was held on the 7th day of December 2010 regarding providing infrastructural facilities.
The Board indeed extended the timeline for the payment of the balance amount.
It has given the go-by to the terms and conditions.
Under these circumstances, the action of the Board is not justified.
The main justification for the legal enforcement of the right by the petitioner is that the Board was under an obligation to provide the infrastructure facilities but it failed to keep up the obligation even after the extension of time.
In my considered view, the petitioner is right in its justification.
There is nothing on record to show that the Board informed the petitioner about the completion of the infrastructure facilities.
On the other hand, it went on demanding the payment of the balance amount with interest.
And on one fine day, it informed the petitioner that it has canceled the allotment of land in plots No.2 Part & 3 with immediate effect.
The Board also informed the petitioner to go over to their office for a refund of the eligible amount as per the rules.
